\chapter{Which One in the Line}
\label{ch:ml-ordinals}
\hlchaptermodality{67}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say first to fifth in Malayalam, and make an ordinal from any number by taking off its final u and adding -aam.}

The five said in order, every one of them built by the ending and not one of them memorized.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[onnāṁ]{\ml{ഒന്നാം} (onnāṁ) — first}

\label{lesson:ML-C67-first}



\begin{quote}
A new kind of number word starts here, so the recalls come first, at the four growing distances this book measures.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{koyttŭ} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nellŭ} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{viśappŭ} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kṛtajñata} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{ഒന്നാം}}
\textbf{\ml{ഒന്നാം}} (\emph{onnāṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{first}\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\ml{ഒന്ന്}, \ml{രണ്ട്}, \ml{മൂന്ന്}} answer \textbf{how many}. This word answers \textbf{which one in the line}, and Malayalam keeps a second set of words for that job.

It goes straight in front of what it counts, and nothing on the noun changes: \textbf{\ml{ഒന്നാം} \ml{വഴി}} (\emph{onnāṁ vaḻi}), the first way; \textbf{\ml{ഒന്നാം} \ml{പുസ്തകം}} (\emph{onnāṁ pustakaṁ}), the first book.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one ending, and no exceptions to it}]
Look at the word against the number it comes from:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{cardinal} & \textbf{ordinal} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഒന്ന്}} (\emph{onnŭ}) & \textbf{\ml{ഒന്നാം}} (\emph{onnāṁ}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The final \textbf{ŭ} goes, and \textbf{\ml{ആം}} (\emph{-āṁ}) goes on. That is the rule, and Malayalam applies it to every number without a single exception — including this one.

Notice what that means about \textbf{where this chapter starts}. English has to teach \emph{first, second, third} before any pattern begins. Latin has ten separate words. Even Malayalam's own sisters make \emph{first} a special case. Malayalam does not, so this book can begin at \textbf{one} and simply count — and it begins there in order to say so.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{onnŭ}, then \emph{onnāṁ}
  \item \emph{onnāṁ vaḻi} — the first way
  \item \emph{onnŭ} is how many, \emph{onnāṁ} is which one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{ഒന്നാം} mean? (\textbf{First} — which one in the line.) What did you do to \ml{ഒന്ന്} to get it? (Took the final \textbf{ŭ} off, added \textbf{\ml{ആം}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[raṇṭāṁ]{\ml{രണ്ടാം} (raṇṭāṁ) — second}

\label{lesson:ML-C67-second}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{onnāṁ}, and say what you did to \emph{onnŭ} to build it — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pullŭ} — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kṣīṇaṁ} — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{upakāraṁ} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{രണ്ടാം}}
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ടാം}} (\emph{raṇṭāṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{second}\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്}} loses its final \textbf{ŭ} and takes \textbf{\ml{ആം}}, exactly as \textbf{\ml{ഒന്ന്}} did.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{cardinal} & \textbf{ordinal} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഒന്ന്}} (\emph{onnŭ}) & \textbf{\ml{ഒന്നാം}} (\emph{onnāṁ}) \\
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്}} (\emph{raṇṭŭ}) & \textbf{\ml{രണ്ടാം}} (\emph{raṇṭāṁ}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\ml{രണ്ടാം} \ml{വാതിൽ}} (\emph{raṇṭāṁ vātil}), the second door.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=violet!6,colframe=violet!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Across the family: the word Malayalam did not use}]
Two ordinals is enough to see the machine, and enough to see what it saved Malayalam from. Its three closest relatives all have a \emph{separate word} for \textbf{first}, and it is the same word in all three:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}first\textquotedblright{}} \\
\midrule
Malayalam & \emph{onnŭ} & \textbf{\ml{ഒന്നാം}} \emph{onnāṁ}, straight off \emph{onnŭ} \\
Tamil & \emph{oṉṟu} & \textbf{\ta{முதல்}} \emph{mudal}, \textquotedblleft{}a beginning\textquotedblright{} \\
Kannada & \emph{ondu} & \textbf{\ka{ಮೊದಲನೆಯ}} \emph{modalaneya}, on \emph{modalu} \\
Telugu & \emph{okaṭi} & \textbf{\te{మొదటి}} \emph{modaṭi}, on \emph{modalu} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Malayalam has that word too — \textbf{\ml{മുതൽ}} (\emph{mutal}) is the same Dravidian root — but it drifted, and in Malayalam it means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{from}\textquotedblright{}, the point a thing starts at rather than the thing that is first in line. So the slot that the sisters filled with a special word stayed empty here, and the ordinary ending filled it.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{raṇṭŭ}, then \emph{raṇṭāṁ}
  \item \emph{onnāṁ, raṇṭāṁ}
  \item \emph{raṇṭāṁ vātil} — the second door
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the second door\textquotedblright{}. (\textbf{\ml{രണ്ടാം} \ml{വാതിൽ}}.) What do Tamil, Kannada and Telugu use for \textquotedblleft{}first\textquotedblright{} that Malayalam does not? (A \textbf{separate word}, from one root meaning \textquotedblleft{}a beginning\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mūnnāṁ]{\ml{മൂന്നാം} (mūnnāṁ) — third}

\label{lesson:ML-C67-third}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{raṇṭāṁ}, and say which word Malayalam did NOT use for \textquotedblleft{}first\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{katirŭ} — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{vēdana} — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bahumānaṁ} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{മൂന്നാം}}
\textbf{\ml{മൂന്നാം}} (\emph{mūnnāṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{third}\textquotedblright{}.

Three was the number the Dravidian family never quarrelled over: Tamil \emph{mūṉṟu}, Malayalam \emph{mūnnŭ}, Kannada \emph{mūru}, Telugu \emph{mūḍu}, all keeping the long \textbf{ū} at the front. The ordinal keeps it too, because the ending only ever touches the end of the word.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{cardinal} & \textbf{ordinal} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{മൂന്ന്}} (\emph{mūnnŭ}) & \textbf{\ml{മൂന്നാം}} (\emph{mūnnāṁ}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\ml{മൂന്നാം} \ml{കസേര}} (\emph{mūnnāṁ kasēra}), the third chair.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mūnnŭ}, then \emph{mūnnāṁ} — hold the ū long both times
  \item \emph{onnāṁ, raṇṭāṁ, mūnnāṁ}
  \item \emph{mūnnāṁ kasēra} — the third chair
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the third chair\textquotedblright{}. (\textbf{\ml{മൂന്നാം} \ml{കസേര}}.) Where on the word does the ending go? (\textbf{At the end} — nothing in front of it changes.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nālāṁ]{\ml{നാലാം} (nālāṁ) — fourth}

\label{lesson:ML-C67-fourth}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mūnnāṁ} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kalappa} — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{cuma} — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{anugrahaṁ} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{നാലാം}}
\textbf{\ml{നാലാം}} (\emph{nālāṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{fourth}\textquotedblright{}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{cardinal} & \textbf{ordinal} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{നാല്}} (\emph{nālŭ}) & \textbf{\ml{നാലാം}} (\emph{nālāṁ}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Written, the change is smaller than it sounds. \textbf{\ml{നാല്}} ends in \ml{ല} with the virama \textbf{\ml{്}} under it, the sign that says \textquotedblleft{}no vowel here\textquotedblright{}. The ordinal replaces that sign with the \textbf{\ml{ാ}} of \emph{ā} and adds the \textbf{\ml{ം}}: \ml{നാല്} becomes \ml{നാലാം}.

\textbf{\ml{നാലാം} \ml{പൂവ്}} (\emph{nālāṁ pūvŭ}), the fourth flower.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nālŭ}, then \emph{nālāṁ}
  \item \emph{Look:} at \ml{നാല്} and \ml{നാലാം}, and find where the virama was
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{onnāṁ, raṇṭāṁ, mūnnāṁ, nālāṁ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the fourth flower\textquotedblright{}. (\textbf{\ml{നാലാം} \ml{പൂവ്}}.) What sign does the ending replace on the page? (The \textbf{virama \ml{്}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\ml{അഞ്ചാം} (añcāṁ) — fifth, and the five in a row}

\label{lesson:ML-C67-fifth}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nālāṁ} — \textbf{R1}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{koyttŭ} — \textbf{R2}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pani} — \textbf{R3}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{vandanaṁ} — \textbf{R4}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{അഞ്ചാം}}
\textbf{\ml{അഞ്ചാം}} (\emph{añcāṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{fifth}\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{\ml{അഞ്ച്}} drops its \textbf{ŭ}, takes \textbf{\ml{ആം}}, and the set is complete.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{cardinal} & \textbf{ordinal} \\
\midrule
1 & \ml{ഒന്ന്} \emph{onnŭ} & \textbf{\ml{ഒന്നാം}} \emph{onnāṁ} \\
2 & \ml{രണ്ട്} \emph{raṇṭŭ} & \textbf{\ml{രണ്ടാം}} \emph{raṇṭāṁ} \\
3 & \ml{മൂന്ന്} \emph{mūnnŭ} & \textbf{\ml{മൂന്നാം}} \emph{mūnnāṁ} \\
4 & \ml{നാല്} \emph{nālŭ} & \textbf{\ml{നാലാം}} \emph{nālāṁ} \\
5 & \ml{അഞ്ച്} \emph{añcŭ} & \textbf{\ml{അഞ്ചാം}} \emph{añcāṁ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Count the work. \textbf{Five of five were built.} Not one of them was a word to learn: you already had the numbers, and the ending took one lesson.

That is worth stating plainly, because it is unusual. English makes you learn three before a pattern starts. Its own sisters each keep one special word for \emph{first}. Malayalam keeps none, and this is the one place in the book where the right way to teach a set is simply to count.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{onnāṁ, raṇṭāṁ, mūnnāṁ, nālāṁ, añcāṁ}
  \item the five cardinals, then the five ordinals, and hear where they differ
  \item \emph{añcāṁ vaḻi} — the fifth way
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say first to fifth. How many of the five were words you had to learn? (\textbf{None} — all five were built by the ending.)
\end{tcolorbox}
